html:
A Buddhist temple on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River at Ayutthaya, Thailand, begun in 1630 by King Prasat Thong. It is one of the best known ruins of the old Siamese capital.

Its plan copies the Khmer temple mountain: a tall central tower, or prang, on a raised base, ringed by four smaller prangs and eight chapel towers along a gallery. This looks back to Angkor Wat. Prasat Thong was a usurper, and building in the style of Angkor helped present him as a great king. Some accounts say the temple also marked a victory over Cambodia. It was built on the site of his mother's house, and the kings used it for royal ceremonies.

The temple was burned and looted when Burmese armies destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, in the Burmese Siamese war. It lay in ruins for two centuries and was restored in the late 1980s. It belongs to the story of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, and of the Khmer Empire whose art Ayutthaya admired.
sum: A Buddhist temple on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River at Ayutthaya, Thailand, begun in 1630 by King Prasat Thong. It is one of the best known ruins of the old Siamese capital.
